books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate
The Whig Party and the Second Party System

stimulus.text: The lithograph shows General William Henry Harrison in military uniform, with a wreath below naming him “of Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs and the Thames.” Published in 1840. In that year the Whigs nominated Harrison, a hero of the War of 1812, for president. After a colorful campaign, which included the catchy slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too,” Harrison was elected. He died a month after taking office, and Vice President John Tyler became the first vice president to succeed to office after the death of a president. (Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13.)
stimulus.source_note: Lithograph “General Wm. H. Harrison of Tippecanoe, Fort Meigs and the Thames,” published 1840 (Library of Congress). Public domain; text paraphrases 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 13. Viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The Whigs' 1840 campaign best shows which change in American politics?

options.misconception: The 1840 campaign was famously colorful, with slogans and rallies, not silence.

options.text: Only wealthy elites could vote by the election year of 1840
options.misconception: By 1840 about 90 percent of adult white men could vote; the electorate was broad.

options.text: The Whigs opposed all popular campaigning
options.misconception: The Whigs ran the most popular campaign yet, with a slogan and a hero.

options.text: Parties now sold candidates through image and slogan to a mass electorate

rationales.A: The 1840 campaign was loud and colorful, not silent.
rationales.B: By 1840 the electorate was broad, not confined to elites.
rationales.C: The Whigs ran the most popular campaign yet.
rationales.D: A hero's portrait, a catchy slogan, and a colorful campaign were aimed at the millions of ordinary voters who now cast ballots.
rationales.general:
1. Name the tools. A heroic portrait, the slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too,” and a colorful campaign.
2. Name the audience. By 1840 about 90 percent of adult white men could vote, so campaigns spoke to the many.
3. Name the change. Candidates were now sold like goods, through image and slogan.
Background: Turnout hit 80.2 percent in 1840, the highest yet, as both parties ran mass campaigns.
Remember: when the voters multiply, the campaign becomes a show.
